questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid stating a specific current number for IBM Quantum Platform's free-tier compute/job limits?
options: Because free-tier access has no limits at all
Because those limits change over time as IBM adjusts its offering, so a specific number could be stale — check the current plans page instead
Because the limits are the same as paid tiers
Because quota does not apply to real hardware
questions.explain: IBM's free/open tier terms change over time, so the lesson intentionally hedges rather than stating a number that could become inaccurate, directing the reader to the current plans/pricing page.

questions.q: How do paid tiers (Premium / pay-as-you-go) typically compare to free/open-tier access on shared backends?
options: They get no advantage at all
They typically get queue priority over open/free-tier access
They are only allowed to use simulators
They receive a completely separate, unshared set of backends with zero queue
questions.explain: Paid plans typically get priority in the shared queue over open/free-tier access, meaning free-tier users should realistically expect longer waits than what a paid-tier demo might show.

questions.q: What is the recommended practical workflow given limited free-tier quota?
options: Submit every circuit directly to real hardware to save time
Debug and validate circuits on AerSimulator first (free and unlimited), then submit only validated circuits to real hardware, batched where possible
Only ever use real hardware, never simulation
Avoid using simulation entirely since it doesn't reflect real noise
questions.explain: Since AerSimulator is free and effectively unlimited, the practical workflow is to debug and validate there first, and only spend scarce, possibly metered real-hardware quota on circuits you're already confident are correct — batching them to conserve quota further.

questions.q: Why is submitting an unvalidated, still-buggy circuit directly to real hardware a poor use of quota?
options: Because real hardware cannot run buggy circuits at all
Because a bug you could catch for free in simulation instead consumes scarce, limited real-hardware quota and queue time
Because buggy circuits are rejected automatically with no cost
Because it has no downside at all
questions.explain: Real hardware access and queue time are limited resources; spending them on a circuit that still has a bug you could have caught for free in simulation wastes that limited budget.

questions.q: Given a limited monthly hardware-run budget and three circuits — one thoroughly validated, one still actively buggy, and one run purely out of curiosity — what does this lesson suggest is the most defensible prioritization approach?
options: Run all three immediately in the order you thought of them
Run the buggy one first since it needs the most help

Prioritize the validated circuit (where hardware tells you something new, like a real noise signature) over the still-buggy one (fix for free in simulation) and the curiosity-only one (ask whether simulation would already answer the question)
Never use real hardware at all and rely only on simulation forever
questions.explain: The lesson's reflection framework is to spend limited hardware quota where it actually yields new information (a validated circuit's real-hardware behavior), rather than on bugs that simulation could catch for free or curiosity runs that simulation might equally satisfy.
